Management addressed head-on the central investor concern of a sharply decelerating energy-drink category in scanner data.
Category slowdown described as real and 'disappointing,' driven by external factors - weather, delayed resets, gas-pump and rising-cost pressure on consumer spending.
Celsius itself continues to grow - if backed out, the rest of the category would be in negative growth.
Celsius's four-week share (June 2 data) is 11.5%, brand up 35% in the latest four-week read; weekly Moolak scans rose from ~$40M in January to ~$50M recently.
Largest reset season in company history nearing completion (~85-90% done) with significant Essentials 16-oz space gains.

Pepsi inventory: CFO disclosed roughly $20-30M of in-quarter Pepsi optimization impacting net revenues, while stressing Pepsi system depletions grew mid-teens versus Q1 and Pepsi is now 'fully' optimized.
Strong multi-line portfolio (Core/Fruit Forward, Vibe, Fizz-Free, Essentials) - no reliance on a single hero SKU.
Reaffirmed 'upper 40s' full-year gross margin framework; framed the back half as a likely reset-driven scanner reacceleration into the busiest summer selling season.
Methodical multi-partner international playbook - 'agnostic about who that is,' finding the right partner to grow and profit together.
M&A and buybacks are active board-level discussions but neither is 'of urgency'; M&A would have to be an easy bolt-on.
Future structural margin catalyst: shipping direct to Pepsi distribution centers (bypassing mixing centers) creates margin improvement on both ends with only 'nominal' days-on-hand noise.

Pricing reticence - management declined to confirm a price increase; Celsius cannot do zip-code pricing and only controls the price into its distributor; NACS October 7 framed as the summer playbook 'finish line.'
Asked why the energy-drink sector has been slowing progressively this year, what the factors are, and what needs to happen to turn the segment around.

CEO Fieldly agreed the category has slowed; forecasts still anticipate good growth and summer is the busiest season. Cited weather, reset timing and consumer spending pressure as factors, calling it 'disappointing.' Stressed Celsius is still growing - backing it out, the rest of the category would be negative; four-week read (June 2) is 11.5% share. CFO Langhans agreed - running the playbook, 12 markets above a 15 share, 20+ on Amazon.
Shelf Reset Progress & Causes of Delay
Asked how much of the shelf resets are in market, whether they are taking longer than expected, what is causing the delay, and when Celsius will be fully set.

Grocery resets normally occur early January and convenience in March/April, but resets were delayed this year - most likely labor shortages. Celsius is 'probably coming towards the end of the resets,' having had its biggest reset season ever with substantial additional space, better placements and space gains for the Essentials 16-oz line. Well positioned heading into summer; the 'finish line' is NACS on October 7.
Noted Celsius appears ~85-90% done on shelf sets and asked whether, as sets are fully in and marketing kicks in, scanner data would reaccelerate in the next month or two.

Said that is the plan - shelves are set for the year with mid-year cut-ins as a further opportunity; management hopes the category shifts to growth mode entering summer. Celsius is at 11.5% national four-week share, up 35%; weekly Moolak scans rose from ~$40M in January to ~$50M recently. The multi-line portfolio is well suited to today's consumer; 12 markets above a 15 share.
Asked how Celsius segments the market across its brand families, how the product lines meet different occasions/demographics, how incremental they appear, and for early reads on Essentials.

The portfolio build-out is working - the Core/Fruit Forward line leans on the better-for-you healthy halo; the Vibe line is more experiential with a more aggressive personality; the Fizz-Free line (three flavors, plus a variety pack coming) targets cold-coffee and anti-carbonation consumers; the Essentials 16-oz line (replacing the older Celsius Heat) addresses the ~50% of the category that is 16-oz in convenience. Mintel and Numerator data show 'not a lot of cannibalization' - Essentials is truly incremental.
Acknowledging it is super early, asked whether any metrics - repeat purchase, demographic data - give early confidence in Essentials' incrementality and success.

Fieldly said it is very early - the longest placement is 7-Eleven at ~five months. Essentials targets the 18-24 male consumer (versus Celsius's historical 50/50 mix) and initial survey data suggests it is hitting that consumer; broader distribution and a full summer are needed for clearer reads. Essentials is now at Walmart and 'just about every retailer.' CFO Langhans added the incremental data shows Essentials is additive to the product.

Noted Numerator data suggesting ~80% of Celsius's growth is from consumers new to the energy category, asked whether Celsius's data agrees, whether those drinkers skew different demographics, and whether Celsius sources more from coffee than typical.

Consumers often do not see Celsius as an energy drink - it is part of their daily routine. Celsius brings in consumers who avoided traditional energy's 'aggressive tone.' Coffee is a real source of new-to-category consumers; 18-24 college students are a big cohort, and Pepsi has expanded Celsius into colleges and universities. Growth also comes from increased consumption among existing users and from consumers who do not drink soda.

Asked how management balances US volume growth versus pricing - given Red Bull's November increase, Monster's potential move and the weaker category - and whether differentiated pricing by zip code is feasible.

Fieldly declined to confirm a price increase. CFO Langhans said Celsius is not positioned to do zip-code pricing the way fast-food chains attempted; pricing varies by venue and user occasion, but ultimately the price is set by the retailer/grocer - Celsius only controls what it charges its distributor. Fieldly said there are multiple pricing levers (promotional strategies, slotting, pack and channel strategies, variety packs) and Celsius will take pricing where opportunities arise; reaffirmed the upper-40s full-year gross margin framework.
Shared strong anecdotal Canada data from a Toronto Circle K visit and asked for numbers supporting it.

Canada surprised management - a four-week read at the end of the quarter was around a 5.5 share after only a few short months, exceeding expectations with more opportunity through summer. It shows the brand scales, citing Sweden at ~14 share and continued growth in Finland.
Asked what Celsius is seeing in the UK after its recent entrance.

CFO Langhans said UK and Ireland are early days, focused first on fitness and health locations to build brand awareness; good brand awareness already in the UK and Australia, helped by global influencer and F1 assets. The approach is 'fast seeding' - timing and sequencing, not a big-bang launch. UK success will be clearest in the back half; early performance is meeting or exceeding expectations.
Asked how management thinks about the long-term international strategy - whether it could mean five or six different partners across markets and multiple routes to market.

CFO Langhans confirmed yes - different markets inherently have different large distributors across APAC, EMEA and LATAM. Celsius is 'agnostic' about who the partner is; the priority is finding the right partner to grow and profit together and expand the brand internationally.
Relaying an investor question, asked how much Pepsi inventory issues have played into reported results and the likely second-half impact.

CFO Langhans explained days-on-hand methodology (current weekly depletions vs total inventory). Pepsi took inventory and days-on-hand up last year when Celsius was new and growing fast, then began optimizing; that optimization (~$20-30M during the quarter) impacted net revenues. Pepsi system depletions grew mid-teens versus Q1, so demand remains healthy. Pepsi is essentially fully optimized; the back half is 'less of an issue' for comps. A future shift to shipping direct to Pepsi DCs offers margin benefit on both ends with only 'nominal' noise.
Use of Cash: M&A & Share Buybacks
Asked for thoughts on use of cash - M&A versus share buybacks - including whether buybacks could smooth the stock's scanner-data-driven volatility.

Fieldly said Celsius is in a strong cash position generating good cash flow; it looks at potential M&A but wants to keep teams focused - M&A is not urgent and would need to be a special, easy bolt-on. Share buybacks have been discussed internally. Noted Monster holds about three times more cash, suggesting Celsius is at a reasonable level; capital deployment is an ongoing board-level discussion.
